name: Aeroterra USA
paragraphs: Everything happens somewhere, and almost nothing is filed that way. A water utility knows how many kilometres of main it owns without knowing which stretch is failing. An energy company holds decades of survey data in formats nobody opens. Geographic information systems have answered this for decades, but the category still reads as specialist equipment — a back room of cartographers, a licence list running to well over a hundred names. The gap is not capability. It is access.

Aeroterra is the authorised Esri distributor for Argentina and Uruguay, licensing and supporting the ArcGIS platform across both markets. The site carries the whole of it: ArcGIS Online, Pro and Enterprise, the server extensions, the field apps used to collect data offline, the developer APIs and the data catalogues. Alongside them sit two products Aeroterra builds itself — SmartLIS for cadastral administration, Yacimiento Virtual for oil-field planning. Two regional editions, Argentine and Uruguayan, run from one structure.

The organising idea is to teach before selling. A primer on what GIS actually is — mapping, spatial analysis, data management, communication — sits at the top level of the site, not buried in a resources tab. Industry comes next: water, mining, oil and gas, telecoms, public safety, each carrying an account of a working deployment. Only then the catalogue, grouped the way the platform is bought rather than alphabetised. The typography stays plain; the contact form routes by sector, organisation type and interest.
pullQuote: The organising idea is to teach before selling.
oneLiner: Esri's platform, in Argentina and Uruguay

name: Por El Deporte
paragraphs: Most neighbourhood football clubs die in the garage. A crest gets drawn, a batch of shirts gets ordered, and the wrong sizes sit in boxes until someone gives them away. The culture is real enough — the Sunday game, the group chat, the people who keep turning up — but the thing you can actually buy is usually an afterthought. Por El Deporte has been putting on games in Key Biscayne since 2014. The shirt is how the club travels.

Por El Deporte is a Miami soccer apparel brand and a club that still plays. The storefront carries the "Palmas" jersey, a hoodie, tropical tees, hats and totes — made to order, free US shipping, about a week to the door — and says plainly on the product page that every order helps fund the next game. One codebase serves the browser and installs to the home screen on iOS and Android, so there is no second app drifting out of step.

The site is built like a matchday programme, not a catalogue. Cream sand, crest orange, sea blue, pitch green. A fat display face set enormous over plain Montserrat. Cards and buttons outlined in ink and dropped onto a solid orange offset, so the page reads as screen print rather than software. The photography does the rest: keepers stretched low, families on the touchline, shirts worn in the weather they were made for.
pullQuote: The shirt is how the club travels.
oneLiner: A Key Biscayne club you can wear

name: SpatioTerra
paragraphs: A water main does not fail without warning. It seeps, it drops pressure, it accumulates work orders and inspection notes and soil records — all of it captured somewhere, none of it in the same place. Cities and utilities are better instrumented than they have ever been and no closer to a shared account of what is actually happening on the ground. A map tells you where. A dashboard tells you what already happened. Neither one can act.

Spatioterra is a spatiotemporal mesh: sensors, imagery, records, models and operational data resolved into one governed layer where every object, event and action carries place, time, evidence, relationships, history and rules. The whole system rests on three primitives — objects, events, actions — read across eight operating dimensions. Signals become operational objects; approved decisions write back into the systems that run the work. AcquaTerra narrows the same mesh to a water network, ranking every segment by risk rather than hindsight.

The site is built the way the product is: one continuous spine of full-height plates, each numbered and labelled, moving from overview to primitives to the eight dimensions to the systems that run on them. Everything is set in a hyperlegible monospace on near-black, with a single accent colour per domain — violet for the mesh, teal for the network, amber where the system acts. Diagrams are live rather than screenshotted; a node holds when you hover or tab to it, and motion stands down when the reader asks it to.
pullQuote: A map tells you where, a dashboard tells you what already happened; neither one can act.
oneLiner: One governed layer for the physical world

name: BMG Kids
paragraphs: Children's clothing is bought by adults for people who will have outgrown it by autumn. Sizes are counted in months. The category has organised itself around that fact — volume, replacement, the endless grid, the countdown banner. A boutique works the other way. Its value is in what it decided not to stock: a floor of Bonpoint, Petit Bateau, Bobo Choses, picked by someone with an eye. Most storefronts have no vocabulary for that.

Boy Meets Girl is a children's boutique in Coral Gables; bmgkids.com is its storefront, running on Shopify. The menu splits four ways — What's New, Brands, Shoes, then Baby and Kids. Brands is a directory, the house list alphabetised A–I, J–O, P–Z, every label with a collection of its own. Shoes are filed by stage rather than size: crib shoes, first walkers, toddler and kid. Sizing on a romper reads three month, six month, nine month.

The organising idea is that the label gets billing. Every card names the brand above the product; the product page opens with By Konges Sløjd before it says anything else. One typeface carries the whole site — Josefin Sans, tracked wide and set uppercase for headings, left plain everywhere else. Product rows alternate with three-up image blocks under centred titles. Sold-out pieces stay in the grid rather than vanishing, which is how a shop floor behaves.
pullQuote: A boutique's value is in what it decided not to stock.
oneLiner: Where the label gets top billing
alt: Boy Meets Girl children's boutique storefront

name: Por El Deporte App
paragraphs: The weekly run has all the apparatus of a real competition and none of its record. Twelve places, two captains, a scoreline that mattered on Sunday night. By Tuesday it has scrolled out of a group chat, along with the waitlist, the drop-outs, and the argument about who was actually on the winning side. Recreational sport is still organised the way it has been for decades: a thread, a spreadsheet, and one person's memory.

Por El Deporte is an iPhone app for a community that plays together regularly. The home screen answers two questions — what am I in for, and what can I claim — with capacity counters, open spots, waitlist status, and a single button on each game. A live draft room runs the pick in real time: rounds, captains, who is still available. When it is over the game closes into a recap with both sides and the score, and the table moves.

The idea behind it is that a kickabout deserves the furniture of a proper league. Every player row carries a form guide, the last five results as W and L chips, so a captain picks on evidence rather than memory. The leaderboard has a podium; profiles keep a rating and badges that fill as you keep turning up. It is all set in near-black, which leaves the club crest and its orange to do the only shouting, and every card offers one clear thing to do.
pullQuote: A kickabout deserves the furniture of a proper league.
oneLiner: The weekly run, finally on the record
alt: Por El Deporte app on the App Store

name: The Grove Art Studio
paragraphs: Children's art classes are usually discovered the same way: a flyer on a school noticeboard, a friend's recommendation, an Instagram story that disappears in a day. The programme exists, the dates exist, the prices exist — but they live in a message thread, and the same questions come round every term. The category has a visual habit too: balloon fonts, primary colours, clip-art paint splats. The work children actually make rarely looks like that.

The Grove Art Studio works out of a fourth-floor room in The Mayfair, on Grand Avenue in Coconut Grove: after-school classes, no-school-day camps, seasonal camps, pop-ups, private lessons and birthday parties, taught in small groups across three age bands. The site puts all six programmes, the hours, the summer weeks and the prices on one page, each section addressable by anchor. Enrolment runs through the studio's registration system; a parent who would rather ask first gets WhatsApp with the message already written, or a phone number.

The design idea was to take the register up rather than down: a fat poster face for headings, a serif for body copy, and a palette of soft pink, deep magenta and teal on warm off-white — the colours of the room, not of a toy box. Children's work carries the imagery, and the gallery is framed as a normal week at the studio rather than a portfolio. Practical things stay practical. The camp grid is weeks by age group, one button per cell, and the directions end with "look for the pink bird".
pullQuote: Take the register up, not down: the colours of the room, not the toy box.

name: Champy's Seafood
paragraphs: Stone crab is one of the few foods that still refuses to be available. The claw is taken, the crab goes back in the water, and the season runs from autumn into spring and then simply stops. Nothing about that suits an online shop. Price moves with the market. The unit is a pound, not an item. And it is perishable enough that the cooler, the bibs and the mallets ship with it.

Champy's Seafood sells Florida Keys stone crabs to the door — claws to your crib, as the header puts it, over a phone number in case you would rather call. Claws are ordered by size: Medium, Large, Jumbo, Colossal, priced by the pound with a three-pound minimum on each. Cracking is its own line item, billed by order weight. Around the crab sit the sides — Claw's Slaw, Mac & Cheesy, Spinach Dippy, key lime pie — and a gift card that stays in stock when everything else has gone.

Nothing in the interface performs. Type is a plain sans, the layout a grid of photographs; the idea underneath is to let the constraints show. Sold out is not a failure state here, it is the calendar, so the shop stays standing through the closed months with its labels honest. Size becomes the variant, the pound becomes the quantity, cracking becomes a product you add rather than a service you phone about. Under each item sit the questions people actually ask: claws to a pound, how to keep the ice from melting.
pullQuote: Sold out is not a failure state here, it is the calendar.
oneLiner: A shop that keeps the season's hours

name: The Mindful Network
paragraphs: Looking for a therapist is a research task handed to the person least able to take it on. The usual route runs through an insurer's provider PDF, a directory last updated years ago, and a list of numbers that ring out. Each dead end is absorbed by someone already at the end of their patience — often a parent or a caregiver, doing the searching on behalf of somebody else rather than themselves.

The Mindful Network is a curated directory of mental health professionals across South Florida. Search filters on treatment type, condition, insurance, therapy, city and age — the six things that actually shorten a list. Each listing carries services, specialties, languages, populations served, modalities and the insurance plans accepted, with a message form on the profile itself. Around it sit a support-links directory, a student hub that opens prefiltered for children and adolescents, events and a blog.

The design assumes a bad week. Crisis lines sit high on the home page as tappable numbers, above anything that asks you to browse. Profiles open on an at-a-glance panel — location, populations served, modalities, the full insurance list — so the disqualifying facts arrive before the prose. Every listing states plainly that it was independently sourced and carries no endorsement. The result reads less like a marketplace than a reference you can put down and return to.
pullQuote: The design assumes a bad week — crisis numbers first, disqualifying facts before prose.
oneLiner: A directory built for a bad week

name: AulaGIS
paragraphs: GIS is not a subject you can learn by reading about it. It is a set of tools — geodatabases, coordinate systems, field collection apps, web map builders — that only make sense with the software open in front of you. Which is why professional training has stayed stubbornly classroom-shaped: a room, a timetable, an instructor, a week away from the desk. The people who most need it are the ones already using the software all day, and they are the ones who cannot spare the week.

AulaGIS is a Spanish-language course portal built for exactly that. The catalogue runs from GIS Primeros Pasos through geodatabase administration, Survey123 form design, Experience Builder and StoryMaps, with the practice done in ArcGIS Online rather than in the abstract. Every course states the same facts up front: module count, thirty days of access, a certificate of completion, a price in dollars. Accounts, cart, checkout and profile sit behind it, so enrolling is a purchase, not an enquiry.

The design idea was to make each course page read as a syllabus, not a sales page. The module list is the spine of it, the objectives are written as plain verbs, and the price block repeats at the foot so the decision travels with the reading. Every course renders from the same fields, which keeps the whole catalogue comparable at a glance. The public pages are server-rendered and indexable; accounts and checkout stay behind the sign-in boundary. The Spanish is Rioplatense throughout — elegí, descubrí, conocé — not translated.
pullQuote: Each course page is built to read as a syllabus, not a sales page.
oneLiner: Professional GIS training, off the timetable

name: Moen
paragraphs: A faucet is one of the few objects in a house touched every day and considered roughly twice: once when it is chosen, once when it drips. For most of the last century the choosing happened in a merchant's aisle, or was handed to a plumber, and the dripping was somebody else's problem entirely. Selling fixtures direct collapses that. One storefront now has to hold the person planning a bathroom and the person holding a worn cartridge.

Moen's store is the whole fixtures catalogue, sold direct. Kitchen and Bathroom divide into the shapes plumbing actually comes in — pulldown, pullout, bar and prep, pot fillers; centerset, widespread, wallmount — alongside showers, toilets, sinks, disposals and Smart Home. Named collections, Align through Weymouth, cut across rooms so a house can be furnished in one language. Faucet and shower finders stand in for the showroom question nobody can answer unprompted: what am I actually looking for?

The product page carries the idea. A model number sits beside the name, finish is a variant rather than a separate listing, and the tabs run Description, Documents, CAD, Details, Product Help, Reviews — so spec sheets, instruction sheets, exploded parts views and CAD files live inside the same object as the buy button. Service is indexed the same way, by component: valves, drains, cartridges, aerators, spouts, handles. A record, not a pitch.
pullQuote: One storefront holds the person planning a bathroom and the person holding a worn cartridge.
oneLiner: Every faucet, and every part inside it

name: Agos
paragraphs: An investment decision is rarely written down in one place. The evidence sits in a data room, the model in a spreadsheet, the argument in email and a memo, the approval in someone's memory of the meeting. Ask, long after the fact, why a particular assumption was accepted and the answer is reconstructed rather than read. Agents make this worse before they make it better: more work produced faster, with the same thin trail behind it.

Agos is an agentic operating system for investment management. It connects evidence, relationships, models, Agent work, review and history across the systems a firm already runs, and holds them as one governed operating state. The system carries three responsibilities: context, computation and control. People and agents propose within assigned permissions; named reviewers approve material changes. Two applications sit on that foundation — Reia for real-estate underwriting, Veia for venture — with private equity and AML review named next. Excel, Word, mail and CRM keep their jobs.

The site is drawn as the thing it describes. The name types itself letter by letter behind a blinking caret; a graph runs beneath the type, dashed strokes travelling its edges so a proposal can be seen moving along a governed path. Motion stops outright under reduced-motion settings. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next carries the prose and Inconsolata carries whatever the machine says — labels, states, connector lists — so a sentence never disguises itself as an output. Dark by default, light on request.
pullQuote: The reasoning behind a position should be read, not reconstructed from memory.
oneLiner: Agents propose. The team still decides.

name: Veia
paragraphs: Venture underwriting runs on workbooks. A cap table in one file, a waterfall in another, a returns view forked from a version someone emailed round. The memo states a number; the model that produced it has since moved twice. Evidence sits in a data room, the argument in a thread, the maths in Excel, and none of the three points at the other two. Generative AI, arriving late, mostly added a fourth place for an unsourced number to appear.

Veia is an agentic underwriting operating system for venture investment teams. A single financing is held as one connected state — evidence, cap table, ownership, waterfall, gross returns — so the Agent, the cap-structure graph, the dashboard, the operating statement and the library all open onto the same workspace. A board carries the rest of the portfolio alongside it. Firms bring their own logic through Model Builder, the Agent or an SDK, and the model computes while the fund still decides.

The design idea is that the page should behave like the product's claim: nothing asserted without what supports it. Running text is Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, a face drawn for legibility rather than fashion; Inconsolata carries labels, figures and metadata, so a person's argument and a machine's arithmetic never wear the same clothes. One teal signal against hairlines, light or dark. Screens run on a synthetic fund, labelled synthetic. The nav — System, Proof, Model, Integrations, Deployment, Control — is the argument in order.
pullQuote: A person's argument and a machine's arithmetic never wear the same clothes.

name: Reia
paragraphs: Underwriting a property deal still begins with a pile of documents — an offering memorandum, a rent roll, twelve months of operating history, a term sheet — and ends in a workbook somebody built by hand. The model is the analyst's. The assumptions live in cells nobody else opens. By the time a number reaches the investment committee, the reasoning behind it is reconstructed from memory rather than read, and checking it means rebuilding it.

Reia is an agentic underwriting operating system for real-estate investment teams. A deal workspace holds the Agent, the model, the graph, statements and library over one governed state; above it, a portfolio board carries the whole book by stage, status and owner. The Agent runs a directed first pass, the model computes deterministically, and nothing enters the current underwriting except through review — source and proposal, calculated consequence, then a named reviewer who accepts, edits or rejects. It runs on Agos, as a managed cloud product or inside a boundary the firm controls.

The site opens with the name explaining itself: I A M, R E I A unfolds letter by letter into Institutional Asset Management, Real Estate Investment Agent, a caret blinking at the end of it. Prose sits in Atkinson Hyperlegible, every figure and label in monospace, so numbers read as numbers. Diagrams are drawn in code rather than exported, repainting for light, dark and phone. Screenshots are captioned with where they came from. A product that will not assert a number without its source earns a page built the same way.
pullQuote: The model computes deterministically; nothing enters the current underwriting except through review.
